prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, which brought atomic frequency standards to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I opened with IceCube first and optical lattice clocks second, but having read all eight ballots I move optical lattice clocks to the head of my preferred configuration. Seven of eight members place it in their top eight and five in their top three, and the colleagues who know the physics best (Lindroth, Johansson, Kroll) give the clearest account of why. The magic-wavelength lattice removes motional and recoil shifts for many atoms at once. This took optical frequency standards to about 1e-18, has been reproduced and compared across many national laboratories, and delivers measurable consequences: millimetre-scale gravitational redshift, tests of constants and dark-matter models, and a pending redefinition of the second. As an experimentalist I weigh a new measurement capability that the community has independently verified more heavily than a result still being interpreted, and this is the strongest case on that test. Attribution is also unusually clean: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice and made the first demonstrations, and Ye's group drove accuracy, stability and many-body clock physics to the frontier. A two-name configuration fits within the three-laureate limit with room to spare.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is novelty against earlier prizes. Hall and Hansch (2005, combs) and Wineland (2012, ion clocks) already cover adjacent ground, and several members flagged this, so the citation must be drawn tightly around the lattice concept and its demonstration to avoid appearing to re-reward the frequency-comb or ion-clock steps. A second reservation is that other groups (Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, and the PTB, NIST and SYRTE teams) made real contributions that a two-name credit leaves out. A third is that I am not an AMO specialist, so I rely on Lindroth and Johansson for the detailed priority questions. Finally, my first choice B029 has a clear discovery but only three members ranked it, and a very large collaboration makes a two-name credit harder to defend.

responses.point: Optical lattice clocks should rank first: Katori conceived the magic-wavelength idea and Ye took it to record accuracy, the field is highly mature, and the lattice clock is the natural step after the 2005 comb prize.
responses.response: I agree on maturity and attribution, and it is what moved me from IceCube to this configuration. I would qualify one point. Calling it the natural next step after 2005 is also the weak spot, because Wineland (2012) and Hall and Hansch (2005) both sit next to this work. The citation therefore has to rest on the lattice trapping concept and the 1e-18 regime it opened, not on clocks or combs in general. You also name Lemonde, Takamoto and Ludlow as part of the story, and I think we should record why they fall outside a two-name credit rather than leave it implicit.

responses.point: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene is a genuinely new quantum behaviour, with a prediction followed by decisive experiment, and Eriksson ranks it first with Bistritzer a possible but less natural third laureate.
responses.response: I take the scientific excitement seriously, and condensed matter is outside my expertise, so I defer to you on the physics. My concern is maturity. Lindroth, Johansson and Mehlig all note that the mechanism of the superconductivity is still debated, and Johansson explicitly calls the interpretation unstable. Optical lattice clocks have been reproduced and compared across many laboratories for years, and I weigh that independent confirmation heavily. I would keep B054 as a strong candidate for a later year, and I would like you to say whether you would accept that timing argument or think it undervalues how quickly the field was reproduced.

responses.point: The Higgs observation with ATLAS and CMS is the clearest discovery, nature answering a sharp question, and the three named leaders can stand for both experiments, though leadership as a proxy for decisive contribution is uncertain.
responses.response: I share your view that the Higgs observation is a fully mature discovery with real scientific weight, and as a detector builder I respect what ATLAS and CMS required. But I disagree that leadership roles can carry the credit. The decisive ideas in a collaboration of thousands are spread across detector concepts, trigger and analysis methods that three names cannot represent without being arbitrary, and you say yourself you have not verified their roles. That makes B026 the hardest of the shortlisted candidates to defend on attribution. I note your ranking of IceCube third and would like to understand whether the same attribution worry applies to Halzen and Spiering in your view.

responses.point: Optical lattice clocks come first because the field is limited by how well we can measure, the performance is near 1e-18, the redefinition of the second is under discussion, and two laureates fit cleanly.
responses.response: I agree, and your point about measurement capability is close to my own criterion. I would add a caution to your remark that Ye's later work is distinct from the 2005 comb prize. That is true for the clock results, but Ye's comb-linked clock comparisons are exactly where a critic will say the work overlaps Hall and Hansch. Your cavity optomechanics ranking at 5 is not one I share. The field is moving, there are several parallel demonstrations (Painter, Lehnert, Regal, Cleland, Aspelmeyer, Kippenberg) and the prize scope is hard to define, so I would not put it in a final configuration.

responses.point: Topological insulators are a clean, general mechanism with a decisive HgTe observation, supporting a theory-plus-experiment trio of Kane, Mele and Molenkamp, though the 2016 prize and omitted Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang and Fu complicate the allocation.
responses.response: The conceptual clarity is persuasive and I cannot assess the theory on its own terms. Two things still keep me from placing B007 first. The 2016 prize on topological phases overlaps conceptually, as you and Johansson both acknowledge, and the missing names (Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang, Fu) are the sort of attribution gap that expert reports often turn into a contested decision. Lattice clocks have a much simpler credit chain. I would still value hearing from you how large the overlap with 2016 is in your assessment.

uncertainties: How tightly the citation must be drawn so that optical lattice clocks are clearly distinct from the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-clock prize.
Whether a Katori-Ye credit adequately reflects the lattice-clock groups at PTB, NIST, SYRTE and elsewhere, or whether expert reports would argue for a different attribution.
Whether the IceCube case (B029) can be defended on attribution given the AMANDA, Baikal and DUMAND precursors and the size of the collaboration, since I would want it as a fallback.
Whether the committee prefers one achievement or a split prize, and if a split, which pairing keeps within three laureates; I do not currently favour splitting.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B042 or the other shortlisted candidates. I should disclose that I work in astroparticle physics and am a member of the PAMELA, Fermi-LAT and XL-Calibur collaborations, so I have professional familiarity with the neutrino-astronomy community around B029 and the gamma-ray and black-hole community around B047, though I have no recorded collaboration with the named candidates and I am not in IceCube or the EHT. If B029 or B047 became the leading proposal I would flag this to the committee as a possible recusal question.
